fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: The Designer Who Skipped Critique
fieldNotes.source: Anonymous design manager at PadhAI Tutor, a Gurugram-based AI-tutoring app for K-12
fieldNotes.story:
PadhAI's Series-B launch event was scheduled for **October 8, 2024**. The lead designer on the new parent dashboard — call him R, three years out of NID, very confident — refused two scheduled critique sessions in the last sprint. *"Calls slow me down, the team will nitpick fonts, I've got it."* His manager, conflict-averse and slammed with hiring, let it slide both times.

Launch shipped on schedule. Within **72 hours**, three problems surfaced that any 30-minute critique would have caught: the *Add Child* CTA was below the fold on the most common Android screen size; the parent's weekly progress report used a colour scale where *red* meant *good* (mapped backward from a heatmap library); and the PIN-setup flow asked for the PIN *before* explaining what the PIN was for, leading to a **47% drop-off** at that screen.

The team shipped **three emergency redesigns over the next eleven days**. The first two were patches; the third was a full rebuild of the PIN flow. R was not fired but was moved off the dashboard team. His manager wrote a one-paragraph addendum to the team's working agreement: *"Critique is not feedback you opt into. It is the cheapest insurance you can buy on a deadline."*

The interesting part: R came back in February having internalised the lesson. By Q2 2025 he was running the team's critique sessions himself — including a rule that *every* design lead must present at least one half-finished file per sprint, *especially* when they think it doesn't need it. The team's launch-incident rate dropped to roughly one per quarter from one per launch.
fieldNotes.takeaway: Critique is not a tax on confident designers. It is the only thing that turns a confident designer into a senior one.

bossBattle.title: Two Weeks to Launch
bossBattle.setup:
Twelve weeks into the **Saral Pay** engagement. The launch is in **two weeks**. Vikram pings you Monday morning: *"I know we planned a critique session this week but honestly we should just ship. Three new screens, all 90% there, can we just push?"*

You know what *just ship* means. Your job is to apply the **3-question critique** — *what is this trying to do? what is in the way? what is the smallest change that helps?* — to the three screens, and decide what gets cut so launch happens on time *and* doesn't blow up.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Has personally been the *just ship* person. Has the scars.

stages.prompt: First decision: **how do you respond to Vikram's *"just ship"* message?**

options.label: "Two weeks is *more* reason to critique, not less. 90 minutes Wednesday — we walk through the three screens with the 3-question loop, decide what ships and what cuts. Faster than the redesign you'll need post-launch."
options.explain: **Right framing.** You re-anchored the cost: critique is cheaper than rework. You also gave a specific time-bounded ask (90 minutes Wednesday). Vikram says yes because the alternative he just proposed sounds vague.

options.label: "Sure, let's just ship. We'll iterate post-launch."
options.explain: Post-launch *iteration* is the polite name for *emergency hotfix at 11pm on launch day*. PadhAI did three of these in eleven days. You signed up to be on-call for whatever breaks.

options.label: "You're the founder, your call."
options.explain: You abdicated. The exact moment Vikram needed a contrary expert opinion, you became a yes-machine. Why is he paying you?

options.label: "Send me the Figma, I'll review async tonight and send notes."
options.explain: **Acceptable second-best.** Async critique loses the back-and-forth but preserves the actual review. Pair with one short call to discuss the highest-impact items. Half-credit because it works only if you actually send the notes by morning.

stages.prompt: Wednesday's call. **Screen 1**: a *Refer a Friend* feature with three reward tiers, illustrated badges, and a leaderboard. Vikram is excited about it. Apply question 1: ***"What is this trying to do?"***

options.label: Ask Vikram to state, in one sentence, what behaviour this screen is supposed to drive — and within how many days. If he can't, the screen is solving a vibe, not a problem.
options.explain: **The first question of any critique.** If the goal isn't crisp, no amount of design fixes the screen. Vikram pauses for a long moment and says: *"...we want users to invite people."* That's not a goal; that's the feature description.

options.label: Suggest moving the leaderboard above the badges for better visual hierarchy.
options.explain: You jumped to *what is in the way* before establishing *what it's trying to do*. You're polishing a screen that may not need to exist for launch.

options.label: Praise the illustrations — they're really nice.
options.explain: Critique is not a feedback sandwich. Compliments at the start of a critique are cortisol-suppressors that delay the substance. Diya's eye is twitching.

options.label: Ask if there's user research validating that referrals matter for Saral Pay's growth model right now.
options.explain: **Sharp.** This is the *what is this trying to do* question at the strategic layer. If referrals aren't a top-3 acquisition lever in month 1, the entire screen is a candidate for the cut list — illustrations and all.

stages.prompt: Vikram concedes Refer-a-Friend can wait. **Screen 2**: the *Onboarding KYC* flow, which works but has 7 steps. Apply question 2: ***"What is in the way?"*** What do you look for?

options.label: Drop-off cliffs between steps; fields the user can't answer without leaving the app; copy that sounds like compliance not a person; any step that re-asks something already given.
options.explain: **Lands it.** *In the way* is concrete: friction the user can name. Naming four candidates lets you and Vikram walk the screens looking for them. You find that step 4 asks for PAN *and* DOB on separate screens (re-ask), and step 6 asks for *occupation* with 47 dropdown options.

options.label: Suggest making the form fields a different colour so they stand out more.
options.explain: Cosmetic. *In the way* is about user-friction, not visual polish. The 7-step flow has structural problems your colour change doesn't touch.

options.label: Recommend collapsing 7 steps to 1 long-scroll page.
options.explain: You replaced one bad pattern with another. Long-scroll KYC forms intimidate; 7 small steps with progress feel achievable. The right move is to remove *unnecessary* steps, not to mash them all together.

options.label: Look at the analytics from the staging cohort — where are users actually dropping off?
options.explain: **Brilliant if data exists.** Real drop-off > opinion drop-off. Vikram pulls the staging numbers; step 6 (the 47-option dropdown) loses 31% of users. Now you have your single biggest target with zero debate.

stages.prompt: **Screen 3**: a beautifully animated transaction-history page Vikram has spent two weekends on. It's polished. It's also the last screen in your critique. Apply question 3: ***"What is the smallest change that helps?"*** With launch in 13 days, what do you decide?

options.label: Ship it as-is. It's polished, it works, and the smallest helpful change before launch is *no change* — protect the launch window for the KYC fixes that actually matter.
options.explain: **This is the senior move.** Critique is not an excuse to redesign everything you see. You correctly identified that the transaction history is *already in the launch-acceptable zone*, and protected scarce engineering hours for the KYC step-6 fix that will actually move retention. Vikram exhales for the first time today.

options.label: Suggest five small polish items — different easing curve, different empty state, different timestamp format.
options.explain: You added 3 days of work to a 13-day runway, on a screen that wasn't broken. The KYC fix won't ship in time because you spent the budget here. You optimised the wrong screen.

options.label: Recommend a full rebuild — the animation library is heavy and slows the app.
options.explain: Two weeks before launch is *not* the time to rebuild. If the perf issue is real, log it post-launch with a measurement. Pre-launch critique should bias toward *smallest helpful change*, not *most thorough one*.

options.label: Cut the transaction-history animation entirely — too risky on low-end Android devices.
options.explain: Possibly true but you have no data to back it. *Cutting* the polish work without measurement is the inverse of the over-polish trap; you traded one untested decision for another. Test on a low-end device first; cut only if measured.

outcomes.perfect: Wednesday's 90-minute critique cut the Refer-a-Friend screen, fixed the KYC step-6 dropdown (3 to 12 grouped options), and protected the transaction-history animation. Saral Pay launches on time. Step-6 retention goes from 69% to 91% in week one. Vikram texts you three weeks later: *"That call saved the launch."* **Diya forwards your message to her own clients as a teaching example.**
outcomes.good: You ran the critique loop but spent budget on the wrong screen, or didn't push back hard enough on a feature that should have been cut. Launch goes okay but with one redesign in the first month. Re-read the lesson on **the smallest change that helps** as the actual hardest of the three questions.
outcomes.learn: You either let *just ship* win, or you ran the critique and turned it into a redesign. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **critique as triage, not perfection**, and the part about **how protecting the launch is itself a design decision**.
